vignette:
Carlos

Carlos sits in the leather chair across from the therapist's desk, his posture rigid despite the comfort of the furniture. At sixty-seven, he carries himself with the precision of someone accustomed to controlling every detail—his tie is knotted perfectly, his silver hair is combed back with military exactness, his hands are folded in his lap. But his eyes betray something else: a wariness that seems permanently fixed, as though he is always scanning for threat.

He was attacked four years ago in the parking garage of the courthouse where he had spent thirty-five years prosecuting cases. He had worked late, as he always did, reviewing files for a human trafficking case. The garage was nearly empty. He remembers the smell of concrete and motor oil, the echo of his footsteps, the sound of another set of footsteps that did not belong. A man—he never saw his face clearly—forced him into the stairwell. What happened there, Carlos describes in clipped sentences, as though reciting facts for a legal brief. He was overpowered. He was violated. He was left bloodied on the concrete stairs.

For the first year after the attack, Carlos continued going to work. He told no one. He told himself he was handling it, that he was strong enough to compartmentalize, the way he had learned to do with decades of prosecuting violent crimes. But the compartments began to leak. He started arriving at the courthouse hours before dawn to avoid the parking garage during normal hours. He would leave his car on the street several blocks away and walk through lit corridors instead. His colleagues noticed he was no longer staying late, but he said nothing about why.

At home—the house he had shared with his wife, María, for forty-one years before her death from cancer two years prior—the walls seemed to close in. He began locking doors obsessively, checking them multiple times before bed. He installed new locks, then more locks. He stopped sleeping in the bedroom, instead spending nights in the living room chair, positioned to see both the front door and the kitchen entrance. When he did sleep, he woke gasping, his heart hammering, his pajamas soaked with sweat. In these moments, he is back in that stairwell, unable to move, unable to call out.

The nightmares are relentless. In them, he is always caught, always unable to fight back, always powerless. He wakes with his fists clenched so tightly his fingernails leave crescents in his palms.

During the day, he is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust him. Sounds startle him—car doors slamming, footsteps behind him, unexpected voices. His body reacts before his mind can catch up. In the grocery store, he positions himself facing the entrance. In restaurants, he sits with his back to the wall. He finds himself studying the faces of men around him, assessing threat levels, calculating escape routes. It is the same analytical mind that has served him in the courtroom, but now it works against him, finding danger everywhere.

He has tried to return to work part-time, but the courthouse—the very place where he built his identity, where he spent more hours than in his own home—now feels like a crime scene. The parking garage is impossible. The courtrooms trigger a sense of exposure and vulnerability he cannot articulate. Six months ago, he took early retirement.

Now, without the structure of his career, without María, without the sense of purpose that prosecution gave him, Carlos finds himself unmoored. He is a man who spent his life seeking justice for others while unable to protect himself. He is a man who has spent four years alone with what happened to him, carrying it like a stone in his chest that grows heavier with each passing day.
